name: United States
status: Illustrative draft: author's judgement from general public knowledge; not yet evidence-reviewed
summary: Strongest on compute, frontier models and research; weakest on shared identity and consent rails.
method: Scored against the same anchors and scoring rules as the India baseline. Items reflect the federal and national picture rather than leading states or firms. Review against current sources before use.

P1.evidence: No universal national digital ID (SSN, state IDs, Login.gov, state mobile driver's licences); FedNow and RTP offer real-time payments with limited adoption; card networks dominate
P1.assumption: Market-led rails, not shared public rails

P2.evidence: Strong open-data tradition (data.gov, Census, NIH); no federal consent-based data-sharing layer; open-banking rule contested; PETs active in research
P2.assumption: Data is plentiful but sharing is bilateral and contract-based

P3.evidence: No comprehensive federal privacy law; consent is click-through and sector-specific (HIPAA, GLBA, COPPA); state privacy laws vary
P3.assumption: Consent is not a shared, machine-readable artefact

P4.evidence: Hyperscaler and frontier-lab compute lead; NAIRR pilot for researchers; FedRAMP and government clouds; CHIPS Act investment; grid and energy limits for data centres
P4.assumption: Capacity leads globally, but shared public access is narrow

P5.evidence: World-leading research universities and labs; large engineer pool that relies on immigration; uneven AI literacy in schools; public-sector AI capacity growing
P5.assumption: Depth leads; breadth across government and workforce lags

P6.evidence: Federal direction set by executive action and the 2025 AI Action Plan; sector regulators active; NIST-based evaluation centre; state laws (e.g. Colorado) vary; no horizontal federal AI law

P7.evidence: Few neutral shared-rail operators; strongest open-source ecosystem; SBIR and other transaction authorities let startups win federal work; deep private capital
P7.assumption: Collaboration happens through markets rather than shared institutions

P8.evidence: AI services mainly in English and Spanish; trust regularly measured (e.g. Pew, Gallup); federal bias-audit requirements narrowed; little DPI-style sharing abroad
P8.assumption: Inclusion relies on markets rather than public rails
